typologies.name: Cash Couriers and Bulk Cash Smuggling
typologies.desc: Physical movement of banknotes across borders or within a country, by couriers, vehicles, freight, mail or hidden in goods, to place proceeds in or move them to jurisdictions with weak controls. Flows may reappear as deposits, exchange house transactions or trade.

typologies.name: Cash-Intensive Businesses
typologies.desc: Use of businesses that naturally handle large cash volumes, such as restaurants, car washes, laundromats, vending, convenience stores and nail salons, to blend illicit cash with legitimate takings. Deposits are inflated to fit the business's apparent scale.

typologies.name: Casinos and Gaming
typologies.desc: Use of casinos, online gaming and betting to convert illicit cash into seemingly legitimate winnings or cheques, to move value between parties, or to obscure its origin through chips, accounts and junkets. Minimal play with high buy-ins is a classic sign.

typologies.name: Charities and Non-Profit Organisations Misuse for Money Laundering
typologies.desc: Use of charities and NPOs, or their accounts and fundraising channels, to hold, mix or move illicit funds that appear as donations, grants or program spending. This typology covers the money laundering angle only.

typologies.name: Correspondent and Nested Banking
typologies.desc: Abuse of correspondent banking relationships, including nested or downstream use of a respondent's account by other institutions, to move illicit funds across borders with limited visibility of the underlying customers and purposes. Payable-through accounts and shell bank links add risk.

typologies.name: Freeports, safe deposit boxes and bearer instruments
typologies.desc: Value is parked and moved in forms that hide ownership and leave thin transaction trails: high-value goods in free ports or bonded storage, contents of safe deposit boxes, and bearer shares or other bearer instruments. Title can change hands without goods moving or any bank payment, so owners are obscured and value can be transferred or revalued on paper. Cash used to buy bearer instruments or fill boxes breaks the link to the original source.

typologies.name: Funnel Accounts
typologies.desc: Accounts that collect deposits from many locations, often in different geographic areas, and funnel the money onward, frequently to another jurisdiction, so as to avoid direct links with the criminal source. They are commonly used in drug trafficking and fraud cash networks.

typologies.name: Hawala, Underground Banking and Informal Value Transfer
typologies.desc: Informal value transfer systems that move value without or alongside formal banking, settling through netting, trade or cash, with limited records. They serve legitimate remittance needs but are also abused for laundering and for evasion of controls.

typologies.name: High-Value Goods (Art, Jewellery, Precious Metals, Luxury Vehicles)
typologies.desc: Purchase, trade and storage of portable, high-value assets, often with cash, to convert and store proceeds. Price subjectivity and confidentiality make valuation and origin hard to verify.

typologies.name: Insurance and Securities Layering
typologies.desc: Use of insurance products and securities markets to place and layer funds, for example single-premium policies cancelled early, or trading, wash trades and account transfers that obscure source and ownership.

typologies.name: Legal-Sector and Accountant Gatekeeper Misuse
typologies.desc: Misuse of lawyers, notaries, accountants and similar professionals, witting or unwitting, to create structures, hold or move client funds, buy assets or lend credibility to transactions. Client accounts and professional privilege are used to distance funds from their source.

typologies.name: Loan-Back and Round-Tripping
typologies.desc: Schemes in which criminals lend their own illicit funds to themselves or their entities through apparently legitimate loans, or send funds abroad and return them as investment, loans or trade receipts. Documentation creates a credible-looking origin for the money.

typologies.name: Money Mules
typologies.desc: Individuals, witting or unwitting, whose accounts or identities are used to receive and move criminal proceeds on behalf of others, often recruited via fake job offers, romance scams or social media. Mule activity is a key layering and cash-out step for fraud and other crime proceeds.

typologies.name: PEP and High-Risk Person Laundering
typologies.desc: Laundering of proceeds of corruption or other crimes by or on behalf of politically exposed persons, relatives, close associates and other high-risk individuals, often through intermediaries, companies and foreign accounts. Such flows may be integrated through property, luxury assets and investments.

typologies.name: Pension, superannuation and retirement-account misuse
typologies.desc: Illicit funds are paid into pension, superannuation or retirement accounts, or into self-managed schemes, to give them a long-term savings label. They may later be withdrawn early, transferred overseas or invested in related assets. Sham employers and fraudulent pension-transfer or early-access schemes can also be used to launder funds or to steal retirement savings from victims.

typologies.name: Professional Money Laundering Networks
typologies.desc: Specialists who launder criminal proceeds for others as a service, for a fee or commission, using networks of couriers, brokers, front companies, accounts and informal value transfer. They run structured, repeatable laundering infrastructure serving multiple criminal clients.

typologies.name: Real Estate
typologies.desc: Purchase, sale, development or financing of property to integrate illicit funds, taking advantage of high values, price opacity and the involvement of intermediaries. Techniques include buying with cash or via complex structures, rapid flipping, and mortgage fraud.

typologies.name: Sham litigation, arbitration and legal settlements used to launder or justify funds
typologies.desc: Criminals use real or invented legal disputes, arbitration awards, court judgments or settlements to move money and to give it a documented, apparently lawful origin. The parties are typically connected, the claim has little commercial substance and the payout follows quickly. Lawyers, escrow and client accounts, and receiving banks are the main exposure points.

typologies.name: Shell and Front Companies
typologies.desc: Use of companies with no or minimal real operations to hold, move or obscure criminal funds, or of operating businesses used as a front to mix illicit and legitimate income. Complex structures and nominee arrangements hide beneficial ownership.

typologies.name: Sports, sponsorship and club or athlete-transfer laundering
typologies.desc: Criminal funds are placed or integrated through professional sport by acquiring clubs, overpaying for sponsorship, naming rights or image rights, inflating player transfer fees, or paying agents and intermediaries commissions that have little to do with services. Valuations in sport are subjective and hard to benchmark, and ownership is often held through offshore vehicles, which gives illicit value a plausible commercial label. Betting-linked payments to players or officials add a match-fixing dimension.

typologies.name: Structuring / Smurfing
typologies.desc: Breaking up cash or other value into amounts kept below reporting, identification or internal review thresholds, often using many deposits, branches, accounts or individuals. It is mainly a placement technique and is commonly paired with rapid onward movement of funds.

typologies.name: Third-Party Payments and Commingling
typologies.desc: Use of third parties to make or receive payments, and the mixing of illicit funds with legitimate funds in business, personal or client accounts, to obscure source and ownership. Includes accounts used by someone other than the holder.

typologies.name: Trade-Based Money Laundering
typologies.desc: Disguising proceeds of crime and moving value through trade transactions by manipulating invoicing, quantity, quality or description of goods and services. Techniques include over- and under-invoicing, multiple invoicing, phantom shipments and use of unrelated third parties.

typologies.name: Trust and Company Service Provider Misuse
typologies.desc: Misuse of trust and company service providers, including formation agents and nominee or registered-office services, to create, administer or obscure companies and trusts used for laundering. TCSPs may be witting, negligent or exploited.

typologies.name: Abuse of Non-Profit Organisations and Charities for Terrorist Financing
typologies.desc: Terrorist groups or their supporters may exploit charities and other non-profit organisations by diverting funds, using them as cover for transfers to conflict areas, or infiltrating their governance. Most non-profits are low risk, so controls must be proportionate and avoid de-risking legitimate humanitarian work.

typologies.name: Crowdfunding and Social Media Fundraising for Terrorist Financing
typologies.desc: Online fundraising platforms, social media appeals and messaging channels can be used to solicit small donations across many jurisdictions for violent groups, often presenting as humanitarian or community causes. Detection combines campaign content intelligence with payment patterns across payment processors, banks and platforms.

typologies.name: Extortion and Kidnap-for-Ransom Funding of Terrorist Groups
typologies.desc: Terrorist and insurgent groups raise funds through ransom, extortion of businesses and diaspora communities, and illicit taxation in areas they control. Payments often appear as unexplained transfers, cash movements by third parties or emergency borrowing.

typologies.name: Foreign Terrorist Fighter Travel and Support Financing
typologies.desc: Individuals who travel to join terrorist groups abroad, and networks that support them, finance their journeys through personal funds, loans, family transfers and cash. Financial signals typically cluster around the preparatory period before travel and continue through remittances to the destination region.

typologies.name: Hawala and Money or Value Transfer Services for Terrorist Financing
typologies.desc: Informal value transfer systems and unregulated or poorly supervised MVTS can move funds across borders using settlement by trade, netting or cash, leaving limited records. They are important to many legitimate communities but can be abused to transfer money to terrorist actors in regions with limited banking access.

typologies.name: Lone Actor and Small-Value Terrorist Funding
typologies.desc: Individuals or very small cells fund attacks, travel or equipment from personal income, savings, consumer credit or small gifts, producing low-value activity that blends into normal retail banking. Detection relies on combinations of weak signals and on external intelligence rather than any single threshold.

typologies.name: State Sponsorship and Commodity Trading Funding of Terrorism
typologies.desc: Terrorist organisations may receive support from state actors or raise revenue by controlling and trading commodities such as oil, minerals, antiquities and agricultural goods. Trade finance, front companies and commodity brokers can be used to convert resources into funds and move them to the group.

typologies.name: Virtual Assets for Terrorist Financing
typologies.desc: Terrorist supporters may solicit and move small to moderate amounts through virtual assets, using self-hosted wallets, privacy-enhanced assets, mixers or decentralised services. Risks are driven by pseudonymity and cross-border speed, balanced against traceability on public blockchains.

typologies.name: Correspondent Banking and Joint Ventures in Proliferation Financing
typologies.desc: Proliferation-linked entities may reach the international financial system via correspondent relationships, nested accounts or joint ventures that mask the involvement of restricted parties. Respondent due diligence and payment-message review are the main tools for detecting this exposure.

typologies.name: DPRK-Style Revenue Generation: Cyber Theft and Overseas IT Workers (Indicator Level)
typologies.desc: State-linked actors may raise revenue through cyber-enabled theft of virtual assets and funds, and through overseas IT workers who conceal identity and location. This typology is described only at indicator level to support detection and screening, without operational detail.

typologies.name: Dual-Use Goods Procurement via Front Companies
typologies.desc: Proliferation networks seek controlled or dual-use items through front companies, brokers and intermediaries that disguise the true end user. Financial institutions mainly see this through payments and trade documents, so detection depends on matching customer profile, goods and destination.

typologies.name: Maritime Evasion: Flag Hopping, AIS Manipulation and Ship-to-Ship Transfers
typologies.desc: Vessels linked to proliferation-sensitive trade may change flags, ownership and names, disable or falsify identification signals, and conduct cargo transfers at sea. Maritime due diligence uses vessel history, tracking data and ownership analysis to identify these behaviours without relying only on documents.

typologies.name: Trade Finance and Transshipment Obfuscation for Proliferation
typologies.desc: Proliferation procurement uses letters of credit, open-account trade and transshipment hubs to obscure origin, destination and end use of controlled items. Document inconsistencies and unusual routing are the principal observable indicators for trade finance teams.

typologies.name: Crypto Sanctions Evasion
typologies.desc: Designated persons and sanctioned jurisdictions may use virtual assets to hold or move value outside the traditional banking system, via exchanges with weak controls, unhosted wallets, mixers and cross-chain swaps. Blockchain analytics, geolocation and travel rule data are the core detection tools.

typologies.name: Luxury Goods and Real-Asset Hiding by Designated Persons
typologies.desc: Designated persons may convert financial assets into yachts, aircraft, art, jewellery, property or collectibles held through intermediaries to avoid freezing. Detection is relevant to banks, art and luxury dealers, brokers, registries and corporate service providers.

typologies.name: Oil and Commodity Price-Cap and Ship-to-Ship Evasion
typologies.desc: Where price caps or embargoes apply to oil and other commodities, attempts to circumvent them may involve inflated or opaque attestations, intermediary traders, undisclosed ship-to-ship transfers and ageing or unusual tankers. Detection draws on trade documents, pricing, vessel data and the quality of attestations from counterparties.

typologies.name: Sanctions Evasion via Shell and Ownership Layering (50% Rule Circumvention)
typologies.desc: Designated persons may retain control of assets by reducing recorded ownership below aggregation thresholds, using nominees, trusts, family members or layered holding companies. Detection depends on ownership and control analysis that looks beyond percentage holdings to influence, funding and benefit.

typologies.name: Sanctions Facilitators and Professional Enablers
typologies.desc: Lawyers, accountants, trust and company service providers, brokers and other professionals may knowingly or unknowingly structure transactions, set up entities or move funds to help designated persons avoid sanctions. Indicators focus on unusual service patterns, pass-through behaviour and the enabler's own risk profile.

typologies.name: Trade Diversion and Third-Country Transshipment
typologies.desc: Restricted goods or restricted-destination trade may be rerouted through third countries whose trade statistics, parties or documents show sudden shifts. Financial institutions can detect diversion by comparing customer activity with country-level trade patterns, end-use information and common high-priority items.

typologies.name: Wire Stripping and Payment-Message Manipulation
typologies.desc: Payment messages can be altered or structured so that names, addresses or purpose fields that would trigger sanctions screening are omitted, truncated or replaced. Controls focus on message integrity, intermediary practices and unusual patterns in message content.

typologies.name: Account Takeover
typologies.desc: Criminals gain control of customer accounts through phishing, credential stuffing, SIM swap or malware, then change details and extract funds. Early detection relies on login, device and change-of-details signals.

typologies.name: Authorised Push Payment Scams
typologies.desc: Victims are deceived or coerced into authorising a payment to an account controlled by a criminal, often under a false pretext such as a safe-account request, a fake invoice or an invented purchase. Because the customer authorises the payment, controls rely on spotting behavioural change and mule receiving accounts.

typologies.name: Business Email Compromise and Invoice Redirection
typologies.desc: Criminals compromise or spoof email accounts to impersonate executives or suppliers and redirect payments to accounts they control. Typical outcomes are urgent wire requests or changed bank details on genuine invoices.

typologies.name: Card-Not-Present and Chargeback Fraud
typologies.desc: Stolen card details are used online or by phone where the physical card is not checked, and some customers or merchants abuse the chargeback system. Fraud rings test cards at low value before large purchases.

typologies.name: Cheque and Deposit Fraud
typologies.desc: Counterfeit, altered or stolen cheques, and deposits of items later returned, can be used to obtain funds before the fraud is discovered. Mule accounts and overpayment scams are common.

typologies.name: Cross-border mule and payment-chain laundering of fraud proceeds
typologies.desc: Proceeds of authorised-push and online fraud are moved rapidly across several mule accounts, payment institutions, correspondent chains and crypto off-ramps in different jurisdictions, so that recall and freezing requests lag behind the funds. Each hop can look unremarkable alone; the signal lies in speed, chain length, data gaps in payment messages and repeated fraud-related recalls. Complements ML-MULE and FR-APP, which focus on single-account and victim-side views.

typologies.name: Elder and Vulnerable Customer Financial Abuse
typologies.desc: Older or vulnerable people are exploited by relatives, carers, scammers or persons holding power of attorney. Warning signs include sudden changes in banking behaviour and the presence of third parties directing transactions.

typologies.name: First-Party and Bust-Out Fraud
typologies.desc: Customers or organised groups obtain credit with no intent to repay, or build up credit lines and then max them out and vanish. First-party fraud may also include exaggerated hardship or false disputes.

typologies.name: Identity Theft and Synthetic Identity
typologies.desc: Offenders use stolen personal data or blend real and fabricated data to open accounts and credit. Synthetic identities are nurtured over time before large drawdowns, making them hard to link to a real victim.

typologies.name: Impersonation, Vishing and Smishing
typologies.desc: Fraudsters pose as banks, police, tax authorities or delivery firms by phone, SMS or email, harvesting credentials or inducing customers to move money. The criminal often spoofs numbers and uses urgency and fear.

typologies.name: Insurance Fraud
typologies.desc: Fraud may be opportunistic (inflated claims) or organised (staged accidents, ghost brokers, fake policies). Insurers and banks may see related payments, claimants and repairers.

typologies.name: Investment, Ponzi and Pyramid Schemes
typologies.desc: Operators promise unusually high or guaranteed returns, paying earlier investors from new deposits or recruitment fees rather than genuine profits. Collapse leaves many victims and often a trail of commingled funds and layered transfers.

typologies.name: Loan and Mortgage Fraud
typologies.desc: Applicants or insiders misstate income, assets, identity or property value to obtain credit, or use straw buyers and inflated appraisals. Mortgage fraud may involve collusion with brokers, valuers or conveyancers.

typologies.name: Mass-Marketing and Advance-Fee Scams
typologies.desc: Victims are lured by promises of prizes, inheritances, jobs or loans and asked to pay fees in advance. Scam networks operate across borders using mass communications and mule accounts.

typologies.name: Payroll, Employee, Insider Fraud and Collusion
typologies.desc: Employees or contractors abuse access to divert funds, create ghost employees, falsify expenses or collude with outsiders. Weak segregation of duties and unchecked privileged access raise risk.

typologies.name: Procurement and Government Benefit Fraud
typologies.desc: Fraud against public bodies and large buyers includes bid rigging, inflated invoices, fictitious suppliers and false benefit claims. Collusion between suppliers and officials is a recurring pattern.

typologies.name: Romance and Pig-Butchering Investment Scams
typologies.desc: Offenders build online trust over weeks or months, then steer the victim into sending money for an emergency or into a fake investment platform that shows fabricated gains. Funds typically flow through exchanges, mule accounts and offshore networks.

typologies.name: Scam compounds and end-to-end scam-proceeds flows
typologies.desc: Industrialised online-fraud operations (investment, romance and impersonation scams, including pig-butchering) run from compound-style premises, often staffed by people recruited under false pretences and held in forced labour. The financial footprint spans victim payments, recruited receiving accounts, consolidation, crypto conversion and cash-out, plus corporate fronts and infrastructure spending that sustain the operation. Defensive framing: this entry lists observable financial signals for institutions, not operating methods. See FR-ROM (victim journey) and HT-FORCEDLAB (labour exploitation) for context only.

typologies.name: Tax Refund and Identity-Based Benefit Fraud
typologies.desc: Offenders file false returns or benefit claims using stolen or fabricated identities and direct refunds to accounts they control. Banks see inbound refunds to unrelated accounts and mule behaviour.

typologies.name: Trade and Invoice Financing Fraud
typologies.desc: Borrowers finance the same receivable or goods more than once, forge invoices, or obtain advances on fictitious trade. Fraud may involve connected parties and weak verification of underlying transactions.

typologies.name: Bribery of Foreign Public Officials
typologies.desc: Payments or benefits offered to foreign public officials to obtain or retain business or an improper advantage, typically disguised as consultancy, marketing, or commission payments routed through third parties or offshore entities. Financial institutions see the flows as unusual payments to or from intermediaries, officials' relatives, or shell companies.

typologies.name: Facilitation Payments and Third-Party Intermediaries
typologies.desc: Small unofficial payments to speed routine government actions, and wider use of agents, customs brokers, distributors or joint-venture partners who may pass value to officials. These flows are often small, cash-heavy and poorly documented, so detection relies on expense analytics, supplier controls and awareness.

typologies.name: Kleptocracy and Grand Corruption Proceeds
typologies.desc: Laundering of funds misappropriated or extracted by senior officials and their networks, often through complex corporate structures, family members, luxury assets and international banking. Detection depends on PEP risk management, source-of-wealth understanding and scrutiny of unexplained wealth relative to official income.

typologies.name: Procurement Kickbacks and Bid Rigging
typologies.desc: Improper payments or favours linked to public or private procurement, including kickbacks to buyers, inflated contract prices, bid rigging and phantom suppliers. Banks and corporates can detect patterns in supplier payments, related parties and post-award flows.

typologies.name: Cash-Economy Skimming and Sales Suppression
typologies.desc: Cash-intensive businesses underreport takings through suppressed sales records, electronic sales suppression tools or diverting cash from the till. The unreported cash is spent outside the banking system, deposited in structured amounts or moved offshore.

typologies.name: Offshore Tax Evasion and Undeclared Accounts
typologies.desc: Concealment of income and assets from tax authorities through foreign accounts, opaque entities, nominee arrangements and cash or asset movements that avoid automatic information exchange. Financial institutions see inconsistent tax residency claims, structures with no clear purpose and attempts to evade reporting regimes.

typologies.name: Payroll and Ghost-Employer Tax Fraud
typologies.desc: Employers or labour providers underreport wages, create phantom workers, or operate short-lived 'ghost' companies that collect payroll funds and never remit social insurance or withholding tax. Common in labour-intensive sectors using subcontracting chains and agency labour.

typologies.name: Transfer pricing and intra-group profit shifting abuse
typologies.desc: Related companies set prices, fees, royalties or interest on goods, services, intellectual property and loans between themselves in ways that move taxable profit to low-tax or secrecy jurisdictions. Abuse is typically visible as charges that exceed arm's-length norms, services with no deliverable, or recipient entities that lack the people or assets to justify the income. Banks, trade-finance providers and corporate service providers see the payments, invoices and structures even if they do not see the tax returns.

typologies.name: VAT and Carousel Fraud
typologies.desc: Missing-trader and carousel schemes exploit VAT refund and cross-border zero-rating rules by creating chains of invoices and trades where the VAT collected is never remitted. Common goods include electronics, metals, and emissions allowances; flows are fast, circular and between thinly capitalised companies.

typologies.name: Forced Labour in Supply Chains and Employment
typologies.desc: Labour obtained through coercion, deception, debt bondage, wage withholding, document retention or threats. Businesses and financial institutions encounter risks via labour intermediaries, suppliers in high-risk sectors and unusual wage patterns. Controls combine supply-chain due diligence with worker-centred escalation.

typologies.name: Human Trafficking
typologies.desc: Recruitment, transport or harbouring of people by force, fraud or coercion for exploitation, including sexual exploitation, labour exploitation and domestic servitude. Financial footprints include accounts controlled by third parties, payments for advertising, accommodation and travel, and cash proceeds moved through money mules. Indicators are signals for victim-centred escalation, not proof.

typologies.name: Migrant Smuggling
typologies.desc: Facilitation of illegal border crossings for payment, typically organised by networks which collect fees from migrants or their families, often through informal value transfer, and spend on transport, documents and accommodation. Unlike trafficking, consent is initial, but exploitation and abuse are common risks.

typologies.name: Online Child Sexual Exploitation (Financial Indicators)
typologies.desc: Financial footprints of the purchase, sale or live-streaming of child sexual abuse material and related exploitation. Indicators are limited to payment patterns and account behaviour so that institutions can file reports promptly; staff must never access, view or retain the material and should escalate to specialist teams and law enforcement.

typologies.name: Carbon-Credit Fraud
typologies.desc: Fraudulent creation, sale or claiming of carbon credits and emissions allowances, including double counting, non-existent projects, inflated baselines, VAT fraud on allowance trading and misleading offset claims. Fraud harms climate goals and investors.

typologies.name: Illegal Logging and Timber Trafficking
typologies.desc: Harvesting, transport or trade of timber in breach of national law or concession rules, including logging in protected areas and mislabelled species or origin. Proceeds often pass through timber traders, export companies and shipping firms, with laundered volumes blended into legal supply.

typologies.name: Illegal Mining and Precious Metals Laundering
typologies.desc: Extraction of gold, diamonds, coltan and other minerals without licence or in breach of law, and the laundering of resulting metals through scrap dealers, refiners, jewellers and traders. Linkages to armed groups, environmental damage and forced labour raise the stakes.

typologies.name: Illegal Wildlife Trade
typologies.desc: Poaching and trafficking of protected animals and plants and their products, such as ivory, rhino horn, pangolin scales, timber species and live animals. Financial signs include front companies mixing legal and illegal trade, payments across source, transit and demand countries, and use of trade documents falsified to pass inspection.

typologies.name: Illegal, Unreported and Unregulated Fishing
typologies.desc: Fishing in breach of licence, quota or location rules, often with transhipment at sea, vessel identity changes and forced labour on board. The catch is mixed into legal supply and sold via processors, traders and retailers.

typologies.name: Waste Trafficking and Illegal Dumping
typologies.desc: Illegal collection, export, treatment or dumping of hazardous or regulated waste, often disguised as second-hand goods or recyclables and shipped to countries with weak controls. Profits come from avoided disposal costs and falsified treatment records.

typologies.name: Account Takeover and Money Mule Account Networks (Cyber Angle)
typologies.desc: Criminals take over legitimate accounts through phishing, malware, credential stuffing and SIM swaps, or recruit and trick people into acting as money mules, in order to receive and move proceeds of cyber-enabled fraud. Networks of mule accounts layer funds quickly to cash-out channels, often across institutions.

typologies.name: Crypto ATM and Kiosk Abuse
typologies.desc: Virtual asset kiosks let users convert cash to crypto with light verification, making them attractive for scam victims forced to pay and for criminals placing cash. Risk centres on structuring, repeated high-value use, third-party direction and destination wallets tied to scams or mixers.

typologies.name: Darknet Marketplace Proceeds Laundering
typologies.desc: Vendors and administrators of darknet markets receive payment in virtual assets for illicit goods and services, then move proceeds through intermediaries, mixers and exchanges to reach fiat. Customers also fund purchases through regulated platforms. Indicators appear in blockchain exposure, funnelling behaviour and cash-out patterns.

typologies.name: DeFi, Bridge and Cross-Chain Laundering
typologies.desc: Decentralised protocols, automated market makers and cross-chain bridges let value move without a central intermediary performing customer checks. Criminals including hackers exploit these to swap, pool and hop assets before reaching a regulated off-ramp. Obligated entities usually observe this only at on- and off-ramps through exposure analysis and behaviour.

typologies.name: Mobile Money and Remittance (MVTS) Abuse
typologies.desc: Money or value transfer services and mobile money wallets move funds quickly across borders, often to cash-based endpoints. Offenders use them to send scam proceeds, structure payments through many senders and receivers, and operate unlicensed or complicit agents. Cyber-enabled aspects include compromised wallets, SIM swaps and automated account farms.

typologies.name: NFT and Online Gaming / In-Game Currency Laundering
typologies.desc: Non-fungible tokens and in-game currencies can be bought, sold or transferred with subjective or opaque values, enabling wash trading, self-dealing and conversion of illicit funds into items that are later resold. Gaming platforms also host cross-border micro-transfers that hide value movement.

typologies.name: Neobank and Fintech Account Abuse via Rapid Onboarding
typologies.desc: Digital-only providers compete on fast, remote onboarding, which criminals exploit to open large numbers of accounts for fraud proceeds, pass-through and layering. Fraud rings use stolen or synthetic identities, bulk registration and automation, then operate accounts as mules or shell receptacles.

typologies.name: Online Marketplace and Gig-Economy Platform Misuse
typologies.desc: Online marketplaces, freelance and ride or delivery platforms offer payments between strangers and large seller or worker populations. Criminals use fake listings, collusive purchases, refund cycling or fake workers to launder funds, receive scam proceeds or rent out accounts. Platforms see anomalies in seller behaviour and payout flows.

typologies.name: Payment Facilitator, High-Risk Merchant and Transaction Laundering
typologies.desc: Unauthorised or concealed merchants route card or bank payments through another merchant's account (transaction laundering) or use payment facilitators with weak sub-merchant oversight. This disguises illegal or high-risk goods and moves funds from fraud, gambling or illicit trade into the legitimate system.

typologies.name: Prepaid Cards and Stored Value Abuse
typologies.desc: Prepaid cards and digital stored-value products can be loaded, transferred and cashed out quickly, sometimes with limited customer identification. Criminals use them to move small amounts at scale, convert cash, receive fraud proceeds and fund illicit purchases, often via many cards or mule holders.

typologies.name: Ransomware Payment Laundering
typologies.desc: Ransomware operators demand payment in virtual assets and then launder proceeds through chains of wallets, mixers, exchanges and over-the-counter brokers. Victims and their facilitators, such as incident response firms and insurers, also create exposure. Institutions may detect either victim payments or operator cash-out.

typologies.name: Synthetic and AI-Generated Identity and Deepfake Onboarding
typologies.desc: Fraudsters combine real and fabricated data, or use generative tools to create faces, voices and documents, to pass remote onboarding. The accounts then bear credit abuse, mule activity or laundering. Detection depends on layered identity proofing and behavioural signals across the customer lifecycle.

typologies.name: Unhosted Wallets and Peer-to-Peer Exchange Abuse
typologies.desc: Value moves between self-custodied wallets and informal P2P sellers outside regulated intermediaries, limiting identity information and supervision. Offenders use these channels to receive, hold and exchange illicit funds. Regulated platforms see the risk at the edges: transfers to or from unhosted wallets and P2P advertisers.

typologies.name: Virtual Asset Laundering via Mixers, Tumblers and Chain-Hopping
typologies.desc: Criminals obscure the trail of virtual asset proceeds by routing them through mixing services, privacy-enhancing tools and rapid conversions between assets and blockchains. The aim is to break the link between illicit source and final cash-out point. Regulated platforms see this as exposure to mixers, layered swaps and unusually fast pass-through.

typologies.name: Arms Trafficking and Illicit Firearms
typologies.desc: Illicit supply and diversion of firearms, ammunition and components, including straw purchases, illegal manufacturing, end-user certificate fraud and brokering outside licence. Financial indicators arise in dealer payments, shipping, brokers and cash purchases.

typologies.name: Art and Antiquities Trafficking
typologies.desc: Looting, theft, forgery and illicit trade of cultural property, and use of art as a store of value to launder funds. Opaque transactions, free ports, falsified provenance and anonymous buyers are common features.

typologies.name: Counterfeit and Pirated Goods
typologies.desc: Manufacture, import and sale of fake goods such as apparel, pharmaceuticals, electronics and auto parts, infringing intellectual property and often endangering consumers. Proceeds pass through online marketplaces, small importers and shell traders.

typologies.name: Cybercrime Proceeds
typologies.desc: Laundering of funds from ransomware, business email compromise, investment and romance scams, hacking and account takeover. Money mules, rapid cross-border transfers, crypto conversion and cash-out services are typical.

typologies.name: Drug Trafficking and Precursor Chemicals (incl. Synthetic Opioids)
typologies.desc: Production and trafficking of illicit drugs, diversion of precursor chemicals and sale of synthetic opioids, generating cash proceeds that are placed and moved through retail accounts, trade, couriers and professional money launderers. Chemical and equipment purchases, online sales and pill-press activity are additional signals.

typologies.name: Illegal Gambling and Match-Fixing
typologies.desc: Operation of unlicensed betting, underground casinos and online gambling, and manipulation of sporting events for betting profit. Money is laundered through bets, payment processors and agents, with corruption of athletes or officials.

typologies.name: Illicit Tobacco and Excise Evasion
typologies.desc: Smuggling, counterfeit and illegal manufacture of tobacco and other excise goods to avoid duty, including diversion from duty suspension, undeclared transit and sale through informal retail. Cash proceeds are layered via small shops, wholesalers and cross-border transfers.

typologies.name: Market abuse (insider dealing, wash trading, pump-and-dump) as a predicate and laundering vehicle
typologies.desc: Securities and token markets are manipulated or exploited with inside information to generate illicit profit, and the same trading channels are then used to disguise the source of other criminal funds by manufacturing apparent trading gains or losses. Typical vehicles are thinly traded issuers, newly listed tokens, linked or nominee accounts and coordinated promotion. The proceeds are quickly withdrawn, moved offshore or converted, so surveillance and AML teams need shared visibility of trading behaviour and money movement.

typologies.name: Organised Crime Extortion and Loan-Sharking
typologies.desc: Coercive collection of 'protection' money or repayments on high-interest illegal loans by organised crime groups, usually from small businesses and vulnerable individuals. Victims often show regular payments that do not match any invoice or service, sometimes via third parties or cash.

typologies.name: Complicit or infiltrated financial institutions and insiders
typologies.desc: Criminals gain access to the financial system by corrupting or recruiting staff, acquiring control of an institution, or using a counterparty institution whose own controls are weak or deliberately bypassed. Defensive focus is on spotting the signs at three levels: the individual insider, the institution's own governance and reporting, and counterparty institutions whose behaviour no longer matches their size and customer base.

typologies.name: Customer Type and Behaviour Risk
typologies.desc: Inherent-risk factors relating to who the customer is and how they behave towards the institution. Covers politically exposed persons, non-residents, cash-intensive businesses, complex structures, reluctance to provide information and negative news. Used as the customer-risk dimension of an enterprise-wide or customer risk assessment.

typologies.name: Delivery Channel Risk
typologies.desc: Inherent-risk factors in how customers are acquired and served. Covers non-face-to-face relationships, intermediaries and introducers, remote onboarding and reliance on third parties.

typologies.name: Generic Transaction Behaviour
typologies.desc: Typology-agnostic transaction red flags applicable across all crime types. Covers rapid movement of funds, absent economic rationale, activity out of line with profile, dormant account reactivation, round amounts and third-party payments.

typologies.name: Geographic Risk
typologies.desc: Inherent-risk factors linked to the countries and regions connected to a customer, product or transaction. Covers FATF-listed jurisdictions, secrecy havens, conflict areas, high-corruption environments and trade-diversion hubs.

typologies.name: Institutional Control Environment Risk
typologies.desc: Indicators that the institution's own control environment may be weakened, increasing residual exposure to financial crime. Covers governance, alert backlogs, tuning gaps, insider risk, data quality and outsourcing. Intended for the control-effectiveness side of an enterprise-wide risk assessment.

typologies.name: Onboarding Documentation and Identity Integrity
typologies.desc: Inherent-risk factors seen during onboarding and refresh that suggest false, altered or reused identity information. Covers document fraud, inconsistent details, fictitious addresses and identifiers shared across unrelated customers.

typologies.name: Opaque Ownership and Control
typologies.desc: Inherent-risk factors where the real owners or controllers of a customer cannot be readily identified or verified. Includes nominee arrangements, bearer instruments, layered offshore entities and mismatches between declared and observed control.

typologies.name: Product and Service Risk
typologies.desc: Inherent-risk factors relating to the products and services offered. Covers private banking, correspondent relationships, trade finance, prepaid instruments, virtual assets, safe deposit boxes and cash services.

indicators.name: Reluctance to disclose beneficial ownership or control
indicators.desc: Customer or intermediary is vague, delayed or inconsistent when asked who owns, controls or ultimately benefits from an account, entity or funds.

indicators.name: Refusal or delay in answering due diligence requests
indicators.desc: Customer or counterparty delays, refuses or gives incomplete or evasive responses to KYC, refresh or request-for-information enquiries.

indicators.name: Unable or unwilling to explain transaction purpose or origin
indicators.desc: When asked about a transaction, the customer gives vague, rehearsed, inconsistent or shifting explanations of its purpose, source or counterparties.

indicators.name: Customer accompanied, directed or coached by a third party
indicators.desc: Another person speaks for, accompanies or dictates instructions to the customer, who may appear fearful, scripted or unable to explain the activity.

indicators.name: Account controlled or used by someone other than the holder
indicators.desc: Signs that a third party holds the card, PIN, credentials or device, or that funds and activity belong to someone other than the named holder.

indicators.name: Customer on a live call while transacting
indicators.desc: Customer is on an active phone call, hesitant or following dictated instructions while depositing cash or making an online payment.

indicators.name: Remote-access, emulator or automation tools in session
indicators.desc: Remote-desktop, screen-sharing, emulator or scripted-control tools are detected during onboarding, login or payment sessions.

indicators.name: Login from unfamiliar device, location or infrastructure
indicators.desc: Session originates from a device, country, emulator or network not previously associated with the customer, including shortly after a phishing event.

indicators.name: Multiple failed logins followed by success
indicators.desc: Repeated failed authentication attempts, often across accounts from one source, followed by successful access.

indicators.name: SIM swap or number port before transfers
indicators.desc: Mobile number is ported or SIM replaced shortly before one-time-passcode-protected actions or outbound transfers.

indicators.name: Credential or contact change followed by new payee and payments
indicators.desc: Password, email or phone details are changed, followed in the same session or day by a new payee and large outbound payments.

indicators.name: Shared device, contact or address data across many applicants or senders
indicators.desc: The same device fingerprint, IP, phone, email or address appears across many applications, claims or apparent customers.

indicators.name: Urgent payment instruction or payment-detail change outside normal process
indicators.desc: Staff receive urgent, confidential requests, or changes to beneficiary details, directing payment to a new beneficiary outside normal workflow.

indicators.name: Rapid resale or return of recently acquired asset
indicators.desc: An asset is bought and quickly resold or returned for a refund in a different payment form, with no apparent reason or improvement.

indicators.name: Customer indifferent to cost, return or value
indicators.desc: Customer readily accepts poor terms, fees, losses, penalties or prices, showing little interest in performance, provenance or negotiation.

indicators.name: Frequent changes of customer or entity details
indicators.desc: Customer or entity repeatedly changes name, address, contact details, directors, signatories or ownership.

indicators.name: Repeated change of consignee or buyer in transit
indicators.desc: Shipments or cargoes are re-routed, re-invoiced or have ownership shifted through successive parties without clear commercial reason.

indicators.name: Pressure to speed up or bypass checks
indicators.desc: Customer or intermediary urges rapid completion, secrecy or bypassing of checks, or leans on personal connections.

indicators.name: Staff override of controls or excessive record access
indicators.desc: Employees override approvals, alter records, access records without need or show unusual relationships with customers.

indicators.name: New account or entity with sudden high activity
indicators.desc: A recently opened account or newly formed entity with little history abruptly sees large or numerous payments unrelated to its profile.

indicators.name: Customer disputes legitimate transactions
indicators.desc: Customer falsely claims non-receipt or unauthorised use for transactions they made, often from their own device.

indicators.name: Overpayment by cheque or money order from an unknown party
indicators.desc: A cheque or money order from an unknown party exceeds the amount due and a refund of the excess is requested before clearance.

indicators.name: Expense claims with unusual gifts or entertainment near licence events
indicators.desc: Employee expenses for gifts, meals or travel for officials around inspections, permits or renewals.

indicators.name: Payments timed around contract award
indicators.desc: Cluster of payments to an intermediary just before or after a tender decision, licence grant or regulatory approval.

indicators.name: Repeated wins by the same supplier with narrow margins
indicators.desc: One supplier repeatedly wins just below competitors or in rotation among a small group.

indicators.name: Luxury asset spending inconsistent with profile
indicators.desc: High-value purchases of yachts, jets, art, jewellery or education by a PEP-linked customer not explained by known income.

indicators.name: Channel used inconsistent with customer profile
indicators.desc: Customer uses channels atypical for them, such as a distant branch or sudden switch to digital.

indicators.name: Occupation or business inconsistent with wealth
indicators.desc: Declared occupation, age or business does not plausibly explain the scale of assets or funds.

indicators.name: Weak AML governance and oversight
indicators.desc: Board and senior management receive limited or irregular financial crime reporting and there is unclear accountability.

indicators.name: Persistent alert backlog
indicators.desc: Monitoring or screening alerts stay unreviewed beyond service levels.

indicators.name: Monitoring scenarios not tuned or validated
indicators.desc: Rules and models have not been calibrated, tested or reviewed against current risk.

indicators.name: Poor customer and transaction data quality
indicators.desc: Missing, inconsistent or incorrectly mapped data weakens screening and monitoring.

indicators.name: Significant outsourcing of control activities
indicators.desc: Screening, onboarding or investigation tasks are outsourced with limited oversight.

indicators.name: Overdue periodic reviews or KYC refresh
indicators.desc: Customer reviews exceed scheduled dates, particularly for high-risk customers.

indicators.name: Inadequate or outdated enterprise risk assessment
indicators.desc: Risk assessment is stale, unscoped, or not used to drive controls.

indicators.name: Insufficient training or low staff awareness
indicators.desc: Staff cannot recognise red flags, late completion of training, high error rates in quality checks.

indicators.name: Slow or poor-quality suspicious activity reporting
indicators.desc: Reports are filed late, are thin in content or the volume is out of line with peers.

indicators.name: Unresolved audit or regulatory findings
indicators.desc: Previous findings remain open or recur.

indicators.name: Older customer on first use with large amounts
indicators.desc: First-time, elderly user deposits large sums, often on a phone call, consistent with scam coercion.

indicators.name: Use of multiple kiosks across locations in one day
indicators.desc: User travels between machines to avoid limits or detection.

indicators.name: Customer recruited online for fake job offering payment handling
indicators.desc: Customer describes job ads asking to receive and forward funds.

indicators.name: Operational-security behaviours at onboarding and login
indicators.desc: Use of Tor, disposable email, burner phones and rotated devices alongside high-volume trading.

indicators.name: Withdrawals to bridge contracts at odds with profile
indicators.desc: Retail customers with no on-chain history send large sums directly to bridges or DeFi contracts.

indicators.name: Account rental or resale signals
indicators.desc: Credential changes, new device and region shifts for an established seller.

indicators.name: Use of anonymising network access to the platform
indicators.desc: Sessions originate from Tor, rotating proxies or VPNs inconsistent with declared residence, combined with high-value transfers.

indicators.name: Rapid sequence of new payee additions
indicators.desc: Many new beneficiaries added in a short period, often to unrelated accounts.

indicators.name: Referral or incentive abuse patterns
indicators.desc: Clusters of accounts claiming rewards and withdrawing promptly.

indicators.name: Card-not-present volume with testing patterns
indicators.desc: Many small authorisations from varied cards, consistent with card testing then fraud.

indicators.name: Account use inconsistent with prior low-risk behaviour
indicators.desc: Dormant or low-activity account abruptly receives or sends large volumes in a pattern tied to publicised ransomware campaigns.

indicators.name: Mismatch between claimed identity and device, IP or voice
indicators.desc: Geolocation, language or voice biometrics inconsistent with the stated identity.

indicators.name: Voice or video call authentication challenges failed
indicators.desc: Callers using cloned voices or video deepfakes during high-value requests.

indicators.name: Applications following failed attempts with edited data
indicators.desc: Repeated retries altering one data element until approval.

indicators.name: Customer refuses or cannot support wallet ownership verification
indicators.desc: Refusal to sign a message, microtransaction or provide proof of control when requested.

indicators.name: Transacting via escrow-less informal chat groups
indicators.desc: Customer explanations indicate trades arranged through messaging apps rather than regulated venues, with irregular settlement.

indicators.name: Retirement certificates claimed for corporate net-zero without registry proof
indicators.desc: Companies or traders claim offsets via documents that do not match retirement records.

indicators.name: Crew payments below standards or via third parties
indicators.desc: Crew recruited by agencies with fees, wages held back, or payments to agents.

indicators.name: Mixed legal and illegal operations blending flows
indicators.desc: Legitimate recycler also receives mislabelled loads and commingled revenue.

indicators.name: Customer talks of winning lottery or foreign relative
indicators.desc: explanations show belief in unsolicited windfall.

indicators.name: Password reset or credential change from unrecognised channel
indicators.desc: Self-service reset triggered from an unfamiliar environment.

indicators.name: Session shows automated or scripted interaction
indicators.desc: Non-human timing, headless browser or scripted API calls.

indicators.name: Payment initiated outside normal approval chain
indicators.desc: bypass of the usual purchase order or approval, or approver working remotely at odd hours.

indicators.name: Corporate login from unusual location or after mailbox rule change
indicators.desc: mailbox forwarding rules and unfamiliar logins precede payment fraud.

indicators.name: Customer unreachable after account reaches limit
indicators.desc: Contact details become invalid and the customer ceases engagement.

indicators.name: Early limit increase requests
indicators.desc: Repeated and quickly sought limit increases soon after account opening.

indicators.name: Many cheques deposited by multiple unrelated customers
indicators.desc: A ring uses recruited accounts.

indicators.name: Multiple cards used from one device or IP
indicators.desc: One endpoint presents many card numbers.

indicators.name: Account created and used within minutes
indicators.desc: New account follows rapid purchase flow.

indicators.name: Victim reports unknown accounts or credit enquiries
indicators.desc: customer discovers accounts opened in their name through alerts or reports.

indicators.name: Customer reports unsolicited call or text from 'the bank'
indicators.desc: contact claims to be from the bank's fraud team and requests action, codes or transfers.

indicators.name: One-time passcode shared or requested during a call
indicators.desc: authentication codes are read out or entered while the customer is on a live call.

indicators.name: Pressure for fast settlement or cash payout
indicators.desc: Claimant urges payment and resists documentation.

indicators.name: Employee never takes leave or resists rotation
indicators.desc: Behavioural red flag for concealment.

indicators.name: Staff lifestyle inconsistent with pay
indicators.desc: Visible spending beyond known income.

indicators.name: Customer complaints about staff handling
indicators.desc: Repeated complaints or unauthorised changes by one employee.

indicators.name: Insider override of credit policy or unusual speed of approval
indicators.desc: Staff-approved exceptions or rapid decisions with limited verification.

indicators.name: Delays or fees when investors request withdrawals
indicators.desc: customers report blocked withdrawals or demands for charges and taxes; complaints rise.

indicators.name: Customer borrowing to invest or reinvesting returns repeatedly
indicators.desc: customer takes credit or rolls over supposed profits and refers friends.

indicators.name: Customer mentions an online partner never met
indicators.desc: explanations of payment mention a recent online relationship, overseas partner, military or offshore worker who cannot meet.

indicators.name: Accounts used as pass-through for overseas scam operations
indicators.desc: recruited accounts receive victim funds and convert quickly to stablecoins or wire abroad.

indicators.name: Customer is isolated and defensive about intervention
indicators.desc: customer insists on completing payments, becomes upset with questions or states friends and family do not understand.

indicators.name: Account holder surprised by refund or victim reports unexpected claim
indicators.desc: customer discovers a fraudulent return in their name.

indicators.name: Borrower reluctant to allow inspection or direct debtor contact
indicators.desc: Obstructive behaviour.

indicators.name: Confusion or fear about own finances
indicators.desc: Customer appears unsure of balances, recent transactions or reason for payments.

indicators.name: Customer targeted by scams
indicators.desc: repeated scam payments or telephone contacts.

indicators.name: Document retention or restricted movement reported
indicators.desc: Audit or customer information indicates passports withheld, workers housed on site or unable to leave.

indicators.name: Customer receiving payments for access to minors
indicators.desc: Account shows payments in return for introductions or access, plus use of prepaid cards and anonymous payment methods.

indicators.name: Requests for payments to be hidden or descriptions disguised
indicators.desc: Customer uses deceptive references or asks to avoid records on payments.

indicators.name: Exit fees or debt bondage reports from customer
indicators.desc: Customer reveals owing large sums to a facilitator, or being pressured to repay.

indicators.name: Chips passed between players or taken away
indicators.desc: Chips transferred between customers or cashed by third parties.

indicators.name: Account with little other activity
indicators.desc: No salary, bills, or everyday spending, only deposits and withdrawals.

indicators.name: Operator reluctant to disclose service model
indicators.desc: Refuses to describe how payments are made or settled.

indicators.name: Policy loans or assignments to third parties
indicators.desc: Rapid loans, assignments or beneficiary changes.

indicators.name: Personal use of NPO accounts
indicators.desc: Transactions of a private nature.

indicators.name: Attempts to avoid disclosure of PEP status
indicators.desc: Customer denies or omits political role despite evidence.

indicators.name: Buyers or agents reluctant to provide information
indicators.desc: Parties avoid face-to-face contact, deal via representatives or insist on speed.

indicators.name: Customer reacts to reporting or ID requirements
indicators.desc: Customer reduces a transaction, splits it, or leaves when asked for ID, source of funds or told a report may be filed.

indicators.name: Frequent amendments or letter of credit changes
indicators.desc: Repeated changes to beneficiaries, payment terms or amounts shortly before payment.

indicators.name: Merchant chargebacks and complaints about fake goods
indicators.desc: High consumer complaints.

indicators.name: Customers sending funds to crypto exchanges after being contacted by 'advisers'
indicators.desc: Scam victims transferring under pressure.

indicators.name: Cash couriering or bulk cash seizures linked to customer
indicators.desc: Customer or associates tied to seized cash or declarations.

indicators.name: Proceeds spent on assets, vehicles or in casinos and then converted
indicators.desc: Lifestyle spending and asset purchases funded by cash.

indicators.name: Sudden cash withdrawals followed by pay-outs under apparent pressure
indicators.desc: Customer withdraws cash and appears distressed or accompanied.

indicators.name: Use of third-party couriers or intermediaries to collect cash
indicators.desc: Cash picked up by runners; multiple deposits by apparent intermediaries.

indicators.name: Bets with minimal risk, such as opposing outcomes at different books
indicators.desc: Low-risk betting and quick withdrawals to launder.

indicators.name: Vehicle or container rental by small firms for bulk transport
indicators.desc: Frequent rental or purchase of vans and containers.

indicators.name: Re-export of controlled items by distributors in transit jurisdictions
indicators.desc: Importer reorders and quickly re-exports technical items to another country.

indicators.name: Advisers instructed to use complex structures after a customer's designation risk emerges
indicators.desc: Request for restructuring after adverse news or risk of designation.

indicators.name: Frequent changes of intermediary banks or repeated reformatting of payments
indicators.desc: Rejected payments are resubmitted with altered details.

indicators.name: Request to hold mail or avoid statements and reporting
indicators.desc: Customer asks for hold-mail, numbered accounts or avoids providing tax identification numbers.

indicators.name: Sole-trader or bogus self-employment structure for large workforce
indicators.desc: Many workers treated as independent contractors despite working under direction for one client.

indicators.name: Cash used to pay suppliers and wages directly
indicators.desc: Owner pays suppliers, rent or staff in cash taken from takings before banking.

indicators.name: High refund or void rates on card terminals
indicators.desc: Frequent voids and cash refunds conceal sales.

indicators.name: Sudden stop of activity and withdrawal of funds before VAT due
indicators.desc: Account activity ceases and balances drain just before VAT returns fall due.

indicators.name: Use of coded language, rapid channel migration or deleted campaigns
indicators.desc: Organiser moves between platforms or handles, closes campaigns and restarts under new names after scrutiny.

indicators.name: Campaigns exploiting a crisis event with unverified beneficiaries
indicators.desc: Appeals created immediately after conflict or disaster events with no known organisation behind them and no verifiable delivery route.

indicators.name: Closure of accounts and withdrawal of savings before travel
indicators.desc: Customer empties accounts, cancels commitments or sells possessions in a short interval without clear purpose.

indicators.name: Sudden change in financial behaviour and lifestyle
indicators.desc: Customer shifts from stable spending to minimal discretionary spend, repeated cash withdrawals, closing of long-standing products or giving away assets.

indicators.name: Activity inconsistent with registered purpose
indicators.desc: Transactions, geographies or counterparties do not match the objects declared in the registration or constitution.

indicators.name: Fundraising claims inconsistent with use of funds
indicators.desc: Public appeals describe one cause while expenditure patterns show little programme spending or large payments to connected parties.

indicators.name: Internal reporting on specific customers blocked, withdrawn or never raised
indicators.desc: Staff or managers discourage unusual-activity reports on a customer, reverse escalations, or reports for a particular relationship repeatedly fail to arrive at the compliance function.

indicators.name: Customs broker or freight forwarder with unusually high disbursements
indicators.desc: Broker invoices include large unitemised 'disbursements' or 'duties' that exceed published tariffs.

indicators.name: Third party has no anti-bribery policy or refuses audit rights
indicators.desc: Intermediary resists contractual anti-corruption clauses, books-and-records access, or certification.

indicators.name: Intermediary introduced by official or customer insists on use
indicators.desc: A government contact recommends or demands a specific agent, with limited competitive selection.

indicators.name: Intermediary linked to a public official or relative
indicators.desc: Agent or its owners are relatives, associates or former colleagues of an official with influence over the relevant decision.

indicators.name: Vendor linked to employee or without verifiable existence
indicators.desc: Vendor has no verifiable address, tax number or deliveries, or shares address or bank details with an employee.

indicators.name: Payments to crypto exchanges or cash-out channels soon after receipt
indicators.desc: Funds sent to exchanges, gift-card merchants or remittance providers immediately.

indicators.name: Same beneficiary reached by many mule accounts
indicators.desc: Graph shows many accounts paying the same ultimate beneficiary.

indicators.name: Cash-out through multiple accounts of same user group
indicators.desc: Proceeds are routed to several accounts sharing devices or beneficiaries and cashed out in fiat by different parties.

indicators.name: Counterparty is a non-compliant cross-chain service
indicators.desc: Flows route through aggregators or bridges without KYC and with no governance accountability.

indicators.name: Payout to account not matching verified identity or declared beneficiary
indicators.desc: Payouts or disbursements are directed to bank accounts, cards or wallets that do not match the verified customer or declared beneficiary.

indicators.name: Funds sent to unlicensed or weakly regulated exchanges
indicators.desc: Withdrawals or flows go to exchanges or VASPs that lack licensing or effective AML and sanctions controls.

indicators.name: Agent with unusual cash volumes or splitting behaviour
indicators.desc: Agent location processes volumes far above peers, with suspicious customer splitting.

indicators.name: Rapid cash-out of settlements to third-party accounts
indicators.desc: Settlement funds are sent immediately to unrelated accounts, often offshore.

indicators.name: Card used to pay high-risk online merchants
indicators.desc: Spend concentrates at gambling, darknet-adjacent or unlicensed merchants.

indicators.name: Use of OTC desks or brokers with minimal due diligence for conversion to fiat
indicators.desc: Large over-the-counter trades or fiat off-ramps via brokers that avoid identity verification, pay via third parties or operate outside strong supervision.

indicators.name: Intermediary or broker with no track record and aggressive marketing
indicators.desc: New broker promises guaranteed returns or urgent allocation.

indicators.name: Seafood sales through traders with no traceability
indicators.desc: Processors or exporters cannot show the vessel or catch origin.

indicators.name: Payments to public officials to obtain permits or bypass controls
indicators.desc: Payments are made to officials, rangers or couriers around licences, inspections, reserves, ports or border clearances.

indicators.name: Beneficiary account name mismatch or no-match result
indicators.desc: Victim-side: confirmation-of-payee check returns no match or close match and the customer proceeds regardless.

indicators.name: Change of beneficiary bank details close to a payment
indicators.desc: Victim-side: supplier payment details are altered shortly before an invoice is due, via email or portal.

indicators.name: Merchant chargeback ratio above scheme thresholds
indicators.desc: Merchant-side: high disputes and refunds.

indicators.name: Transaction laundering through front merchants
indicators.desc: A merchant processes sales for undisclosed businesses, or customers use merchants whose profile suggests card-cash-out or third-party processing.

indicators.name: Repeated claims across insurers by linked parties
indicators.desc: Same people, vehicles or addresses appear in multiple claims.

indicators.name: Repair or medical invoices inflated or from linked providers
indicators.desc: Providers submit pattern-bearing invoices with unusual pricing.

indicators.name: Broker or intermediary with unusual early default rate
indicators.desc: Applications from one source show disproportionate early payment default or document anomalies.

indicators.name: Unlicensed or cloned operator receiving payments
indicators.desc: Payments go to operators, platforms or merchants that are absent from regulatory registers, imitate a legitimate firm, or process under a disguised merchant category.

indicators.name: Rotation of winning bidders
indicators.desc: Contracts win in turn across a small group.

indicators.name: Official has undisclosed relationship with supplier
indicators.desc: Conflict of interest appears from registry or declarations.

indicators.name: Invoices from related parties with round values
indicators.desc: Counterparties share ownership and amounts look artificial.

indicators.name: Debtor denies or cannot confirm the invoice
indicators.desc: Obligor verification fails.

indicators.name: Payments to platforms flagged for illegal content
indicators.desc: Payments to websites, hosting or payment accounts identified in intelligence as selling abuse material.

indicators.name: Document fraud service payments
indicators.desc: Payments to document brokers, translators and forged document suppliers.

indicators.name: Travel and visa fee payments for groups from the same recruiter
indicators.desc: Bulk payments for flights, visas and recruitment fees to a labour recruiter, sometimes debt-financed.

indicators.name: Respondent serves undisclosed downstream institutions
indicators.desc: Respondent provides access to its account for other banks or payment firms (nesting) without disclosure.

indicators.name: Many unrelated depositors paying into one account
indicators.desc: Numerous unconnected individuals make deposits into the same account, often in similar amounts or within short windows.

indicators.name: Auction or intermediary used to obscure parties
indicators.desc: Agents or anonymous bidding.

indicators.name: Shared devices, IP addresses or contact details across accounts
indicators.desc: Multiple unrelated accounts share devices, phone numbers, email or addresses.

indicators.name: Large payments from state entities or contractors
indicators.desc: Receipts from government bodies, state-owned firms or contractors linked to PEP's remit.

indicators.name: Use of intermediaries and agents to handle funds
indicators.desc: Lawyers, brokers or fixers move funds on behalf of PEP.

indicators.name: Bank accounts opened or operated by TCSP staff
indicators.desc: TCSP is signatory or conduit for client funds.

indicators.name: Transfers pass through accounts of relatives or employees
indicators.desc: Staff or family accounts used for business flows.

indicators.name: Brokers or dealers lacking licences or end-user certificates
indicators.desc: Intermediary arranges transfers without export licences.

indicators.name: Payments from or to sanctioned or embargoed parties
indicators.desc: Counterparties on arms embargo or sanctions lists.

indicators.name: Seller is dealer new to market or with sanctions or adverse media
indicators.desc: Unknown or suspect dealer.

indicators.name: Importer of brand-name goods with no distribution authorisation
indicators.desc: No authorisation or licence from brand owner.

indicators.name: Import-export firms trading chemicals with unusual consignees
indicators.desc: Importers deal with unfamiliar overseas parties in high-risk corridors for precursor sources.

indicators.name: Players or officials receive payments from betting-linked parties
indicators.desc: Payments to athletes, referees from unrelated parties.

indicators.name: Illegal factory equipment or leaf purchases
indicators.desc: Orders for tobacco-making machinery, paper, filters.

indicators.name: Respondent processing for front companies of concern in prior reports
indicators.desc: Respondent's customers appear in prior internal or external reports.

indicators.name: Exposure to wallets attributed to designated, stolen-fund or illicit actors
indicators.desc: Customer transacts directly or near-directly with blockchain addresses attributed by sanctions lists or analytics to designated persons, thefts, ransomware or terrorist fundraising.

indicators.name: Adviser or agent acting for multiple linked clients
indicators.desc: A single provider, broker, lawyer or agent sets up entities or handles transactions for many related clients with similar structures.

indicators.name: Family members or close associates acquiring assets and positions
indicators.desc: Relatives or known associates assume ownership or management of designated person's holdings.

indicators.name: Sender or intermediary with history of message-quality deficiencies
indicators.desc: Peer institution frequently sends payments with data gaps.

indicators.name: Crisis consultancy or ransom-response payments without documentation
indicators.desc: Payments to intermediaries described as negotiators or consultants with limited contracts or oversight.

indicators.name: Dealings with known facilitators or persons on investigative watch lists
indicators.desc: Customer transacts, including in small amounts, with persons identified in public or law-enforcement material as facilitators or subjects of prior reports.

indicators.name: Transactions involving entities tied to state support for designated groups
indicators.desc: Counterparties publicly linked, by credible reports, to government support for terrorist organisations.

indicators.name: Use of intermediaries who market secrecy
indicators.desc: Customer introduced by advisers or promoters advertising confidentiality or tax-free outcomes.

indicators.name: Payments from or to unrelated third parties
indicators.desc: Funds are paid or received, or instructions are given to pay, through parties with no evident link to the customer, contract, debt or insured interest. Includes third-party cheques, loan repayments, premiums, gaming funds and goods payments not matching the documentation.

indicators.name: Adverse media or intelligence linking counterparties to criminal activity
indicators.desc: Counterparties, suppliers, respondents or controllers appear in adverse media, law-enforcement notices or intelligence connected to financial crime, abuse, forced labour or organised crime.

indicators.name: Repeated fraud recalls or return requests against the same receiving account or originating institution
indicators.desc: A receiving account, or flows from a given originating institution, attract multiple recall, return or fraud-notification requests in a short period, often followed by funds already having left.

indicators.name: Counterparty institution slow or unresponsive to fraud recall and information requests
indicators.desc: A correspondent, payment institution or exchange repeatedly fails to act on freeze, recall or request-for-information messages in time, or the same beneficiary institution appears in many fraud cases.

indicators.name: Dispute or award between related parties resolved quickly without contest
indicators.desc: A claim, arbitration or judgment is brought between parties that are linked by ownership, control, address or advisers, and it ends in a consent order, uncontested default or quick award with immediate payment.

indicators.name: Wealth or spending inconsistent with known means
indicators.desc: Assets, lifestyle spending or purchases clearly exceed the customer's known legitimate income or declared wealth, with no verifiable source.

indicators.name: Account activity inconsistent with declared occupation or income
indicators.desc: Turnover or volumes materially exceed what the customer's declared occupation, income, age or circumstances would support.

indicators.name: Adverse media on customer or associates
indicators.desc: Credible negative news, enforcement notices or investigations link the customer, its owners or associates to criminal, corrupt or regulated-sector misconduct.

indicators.name: Prior regulatory, criminal or enforcement history
indicators.desc: Customer or principal has previous convictions, enforcement or disciplinary action, or has been exited by another institution.

indicators.name: Missing, misused or unverifiable licence or registration
indicators.desc: Customer offering a regulated or permitted activity cannot evidence the required licence or registration, or operates under a licence held by another party.

indicators.name: Account collecting funds from many unrelated payers
indicators.desc: A single account receives payments from numerous unrelated senders with no evident commercial or family link to the holder.

indicators.name: Multiple customers sharing contact details or addresses
indicators.desc: Unrelated customers or applicants share the same phone, email, address, device or bank account, including mail drops and shared accommodation.

indicators.name: One person holding multiple identities or accounts
indicators.desc: The same individual appears under different names or opens several accounts or wallets, directly or through an intermediary.

indicators.name: Inconsistent or synthetic identity data at onboarding
indicators.desc: Identity documents, contact details, geolocation or device data do not align, suggesting fabricated, stolen or misrepresented identity.

indicators.name: Newly established customer with rapid high-value activity
indicators.desc: A recently formed customer with little history or track record quickly records large turnover or trades in high-value or restricted goods.

indicators.name: No evidence of real operations
indicators.desc: Business shows little or no staff, premises, web presence or client base consistent with its stated activities and turnover.

indicators.name: Business revenue inconsistent with staffing or operating costs
indicators.desc: Reported revenue, payroll or resident staff do not match the typical costs and workforce of the stated business model.

indicators.name: Cash-intensive business
indicators.desc: Customer's business relies heavily on cash receipts, making revenue difficult to verify against stock, costs or card use.

indicators.name: Recent change of contact or delivery details
indicators.desc: Email, phone, address or statement delivery details are changed, especially shortly before unusual activity or redirecting mail to a third party.

indicators.name: Accounts held via family members or associates
indicators.desc: Funds and assets move through spouses, children, in-laws or business partners who have no obvious independent source of wealth.

indicators.name: Politically exposed person as customer or controller
indicators.desc: The customer, a beneficial owner or a controller is a domestic or foreign PEP, or a family member or close associate of one.

indicators.name: Non-resident customer without clear rationale
indicators.desc: Customer resides outside the institution's market and cannot explain why they need an account or service here.

indicators.name: Customer in a high-risk sector
indicators.desc: Customer operates in a sector with elevated misuse risk, such as precious metals, gambling, crypto, arms, or money transfer.

indicators.name: Customer claims to be a DeFi developer or protocol team without evidence
indicators.desc: Large treasury-type movements from a stated protocol with no verifiable entity, audits or governance record.

indicators.name: Account opened for a young or elderly person but controlled by another
indicators.desc: Behaviour and device suggest a controller other than the account holder.

indicators.name: Marketplace sellers with no identity verification receiving large payouts
indicators.desc: Pseudonymous sellers withdraw significant proceeds to fiat or exchange wallets.

indicators.name: Corporate account pays an unusual crypto purchase after a cyber event
indicators.desc: Business customer suddenly funds a crypto purchase beyond normal activity, with mention of an IT incident or urgent deadline.
